body:
Why Gujarat is an important recovery example

The earthquake that struck Gujarat on 26 January 2001 caused extensive destruction, particularly in Kutch. The disaster created an enormous need for housing reconstruction, restoration of public infrastructure and rehabilitation of affected communities.

It also prompted Gujarat to strengthen the institutions and policies responsible for disaster management.

Creation of the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) was established on 8 February 2001, shortly after the earthquake. It was initially registered as a society and was responsible for coordinating rehabilitation and reconstruction while also planning preparedness and mitigation activities.

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003 strengthened the legal basis for managing disasters, including mitigation, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

The Gujarat Legislative Assembly passed the relevant bill on 28 March 2003, and the Act came into force on 13 May 2003. The statutory GSDMA came into existence on 1 September 2003.

These dates show that the authority was first created in 2001 and subsequently acquired its statutory form under the 2003 legislation. The 2 developments should not be confused.

Owner-driven housing reconstruction

An important feature of Gujarat's earthquake recovery was the use of owner-driven reconstruction. Under this approach, affected households could take responsibility for rebuilding or repairing their homes, supported by financial assistance and technical guidance.

Owner-driven reconstruction differs from a purely contractor-driven programme in which households have little control over the design and rebuilding process.

The Gujarat experience demonstrated the value of combining:

  • Household participation: affected families could influence rebuilding according to their needs and circumstances.
  • Financial assistance: eligible households received support for repair or reconstruction.
  • Technical assistance: safer construction principles and guidance supported rebuilding.
  • Institutional coordination: government agencies and other participating organisations supported implementation.
  • Community involvement: local participation helped address settlement-level needs and preferences.

Owner-driven does not mean technically unregulated. Household choice and participation can coexist with construction standards, technical advice, verification and appropriate public oversight.

Recovery beyond housing

Gujarat's reconstruction programme also addressed public buildings, roads, irrigation, economic rehabilitation and institutional capacity for managing future disasters. This wider approach matters because families cannot fully resume normal life through housing assistance alone.

The case illustrates the central relationship between reconstruction, participation and long-term risk reduction. Recovery becomes more effective when residents help shape decisions and when rebuilt assets are less vulnerable to future hazards.

Prelims focus

  • The major Gujarat earthquake occurred on 26 January 2001.
  • GSDMA was established on 8 February 2001.
  • The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act was passed by the Assembly in March 2003 and came into force in May 2003.
  • The statutory GSDMA came into existence on 1 September 2003.
  • Owner-driven reconstruction involves household participation supported by finance and technical guidance.
  • Trap: GSDMA was not first established by the national Disaster Management Act, 2005.

[Sources: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, About Us, institutional history and statutory status; GSDMA, Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, legislative history and commencement; GSDMA, Gujarat Earthquake Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Policy, overview; World Bank, Safer Homes, Stronger Communities: A Handbook for Reconstructing after Natural Disasters, Gujarat earthquake housing reconstruction case study (2010). Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A family rebuilds a house in earthquake-affected Kutch while workers and a technical adviser inspect reinforced construction near damaged homes.
pictures.caption: Reconstruction in earthquake-affected Kutch involved households, technical workers and public institutions.

pictures.alt: Household decisions, financial assistance and technical guidance combine under government and partner oversight to produce safer housing that meets household needs.
pictures.caption: Owner-driven reconstruction combines household choice with financial support and safety guidance.

title: Gujarat's 2001 Earthquake: Lessons in Rehabilitation and Reconstruction

body:
Why disasters create financial problems

A disaster can produce large expenditure at the very time that households, businesses and governments experience reduced income. The government may need to finance immediate assistance, temporary services, repairs and reconstruction. At the same time, tax collections may decline if business activity is interrupted.

Disaster risk finance refers to arrangements for obtaining and using financial resources to manage the economic consequences of disasters, including funding response and recovery and protecting affected people and public finances.

Disaster risk finance does not itself prevent an earthquake, flood or cyclone. Its principal financial purpose is to make resources available when they are needed and to reduce the disruption caused by unexpected expenditure.

Finance arranged before and after a disaster

A central distinction is between ex ante and ex post financing.

ApproachTimingExamples
Ex ante financingArranged before a disaster.Budget provisions, dedicated disaster funds, insurance and pre-arranged contingent credit.
Ex post financingMobilised after a disaster.Additional budget allocations, emergency borrowing, donations and expenditure reallocation.

Ex ante arrangements can make funding more predictable. Ex post measures may still be necessary when a disaster exceeds expected needs, but they can take time to arrange and may interrupt other public programmes.

Budgetary provisions and dedicated disaster funds

A government budget sets out estimated receipts and expenditure for a financial year. In India, the Union's Annual Financial Statement is presented under Article 112 of the Constitution. The financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March.

Disaster-related expenditure may be included in ordinary departmental budgets, special programmes or dedicated funds governed by specific rules. Dedicated funds help establish a more reliable source of financing, but their use remains subject to the purposes and conditions laid down for them.

Public spending can be classified according to its economic nature. For example, payments for temporary services may be revenue expenditure, while government expenditure that creates a qualifying physical asset may be capital expenditure. However, the precise budget classification depends on accounting rules and the nature of the transaction.

The constitutional Contingency Fund

Article 267 of the Constitution provides for Contingency Funds to meet unforeseen expenditure before the legislature formally authorises that expenditure.

  • Article 267(1): Parliament may establish the Contingency Fund of India by law. It is placed at the disposal of the President for advances to meet unforeseen expenditure pending parliamentary authorisation under Article 115 or Article 116.
  • Article 267(2): A State Legislature may establish a Contingency Fund of the State by law. It is placed at the disposal of the Governor for advances pending legislative authorisation under Article 205 or Article 206.

The Contingency Fund is in the nature of an imprest, meaning a sum maintained for advances that is replenished from the Union or State Consolidated Fund, as applicable, after legislative authorisation of the expenditure through an appropriation law. It provides temporary financial flexibility; it is not an unlimited source of new revenue.

Contingency Fund versus disaster fund: A constitutional Contingency Fund addresses unforeseen expenditure generally. A dedicated disaster response or mitigation fund has purposes and conditions specific to disaster management. The 2 should not be treated as interchangeable.

Financial liquidity and the total cost of recovery

Liquidity means having money available when payments must be made. A government may have the ability to raise money eventually but still lack sufficient immediate liquidity after a severe disaster.

For this reason, disaster finance must consider both:

  • Short-term liquidity: resources for urgent assistance, temporary services and early restoration.
  • Long-term financing: resources for permanent reconstruction, livelihood rehabilitation and risk reduction.

Insurance, reserves and contingent credit can help with immediate liquidity, but none automatically covers the complete cost of rebuilding. Long-term reconstruction normally requires planned expenditure and careful prioritisation.

Prelims focus

  • Ex ante financing is arranged before a disaster; ex post financing is mobilised afterward.
  • Article 112 concerns the Union Annual Financial Statement.
  • Article 267(1) concerns the Contingency Fund of India.
  • Article 267(2) concerns State Contingency Funds.
  • The Union Contingency Fund is placed at the disposal of the President; the State fund is placed at the disposal of the Governor.
  • Trap: A Contingency Fund advance does not remove the requirement for subsequent legislative authorisation.

[Sources: Constitution of India, Articles 112, 267(1) and 267(2); NCERT, Introductory Macroeconomics, Class 12, chapter 5, Government Budget and the Economy, section 5.1, reprint 2026–27; World Bank, Disaster Risk Finance and Insurance, overview and risk-financing approaches. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Finance is arranged before a disaster; additional finance may follow as needs shift from immediate liquidity to recovery and longer-term reconstruction.
pictures.caption: Disaster finance combines resources prepared in advance with additional financing arranged after an event.

title: Disaster Finance: Budgets, Reserves and Contingency Arrangements

body:
The legal foundation of disaster funding

The Disaster Management Act, 2005, as amended, provides a framework for disaster-management institutions and funds. The Act distinguishes funds for response from funds for mitigation.

Response-related financing meets eligible needs arising from disasters, while mitigation financing seeks to reduce the risk or impact of disasters. Specific expenditure is governed by the applicable operational guidelines.

National and State disaster funds

FundLegal provisionPrincipal role
National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF)Section 46National financing for eligible aspects of disaster management, including supplementary assistance according to applicable guidelines.
National Disaster Mitigation Fund (NDMF)Section 47Financing eligible disaster risk mitigation measures at the national level.
State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF)Section 48(1)(a)Primary State-level fund for eligible disaster response and other permitted recovery-related expenditure.
State Disaster Mitigation Fund (SDMF)Section 48(1)(c)State-level financing for eligible mitigation, preparedness and capacity-building measures.

Section 48 also provides for a District Disaster Response Fund under clause (b) and a District Disaster Mitigation Fund under clause (d). These should not be confused with the State or national funds.

NDRF has 2 different meanings in Indian disaster management. The National Disaster Response Fund is a financial fund under Section 46. The National Disaster Response Force is a specialist response force under Section 44. Their common abbreviation does not make them the same institution.

How the State and Union levels are connected

State governments have the primary responsibility for responding to disasters within their jurisdictions. The SDRF is a principal source of eligible State-level assistance. In disasters of severe nature, supplementary assistance may be provided through the national response-funding system in accordance with the relevant assessment, approval and expenditure rules. For supplementary response and relief assistance, an Inter-Ministerial Central Team assesses damage and relief requirements, the Sub-Committee of the National Executive Committee examines its report, and the High-Level Committee chaired by the Union Home Minister approves assistance.

National assistance is not the same as an automatic, unrestricted reimbursement of every loss. The applicable guidelines determine eligible activities and the conditions for releasing assistance. Similarly, relief assistance to an affected household is not necessarily full compensation for the household's total economic loss.

Sixteenth Finance Commission: 2026–27 to 2030–31

The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended disaster-management financing for the 5-year award period from 2026–27 to 2030–31. Its report distinguishes the State Disaster Response Fund from the State Disaster Mitigation Fund and recommends an 80:20 allocation between them.

Allocation categoryRecommended amountShare of State funds
State Disaster Response Fund₹1,63,521 crore80%
State Disaster Mitigation Fund₹40,880 crore20%
Combined State disaster-management funds₹2,04,401 crore100%

These figures are award-period allocations recommended for 2026–27 to 2030–31, not expenditure already incurred or payments made to disaster victims. The Ministry of Home Affairs issued operational guidelines for the relevant funding arrangements on 31 July 2026.

What changed in the 2026–31 funding approach?

Under the Sixteenth Finance Commission framework, the SDRF has 2 broad expenditure windows: Response and Relief and Recovery and Reconstruction. The Commission recommended flexibility for States to allocate SDRF resources between these windows, while keeping SDRF and SDMF as separate funds.

Preparedness and Capacity Building are placed within the mitigation-fund framework for the 2026–31 award period. This reflects their purpose of reducing the effects of future disasters rather than paying for damage after an event.

The Ministry of Home Affairs' 2026 SDMF guidelines identify eligible activities such as disaster mitigation measures, hazard-specific preparedness, awareness and capacity building, subject to the stated conditions. General beautification or ordinary expenditure unrelated to eligible disaster-risk reduction is not automatically permissible.

Centre–State sharing

For the ordinary State allocations under SDRF and SDMF, the Union contributes 75% and the State contributes 25%. This is the applicable general arrangement for Gujarat.

For the specified North-Eastern and Hilly States, the corresponding sharing arrangement is 90% Union contribution and 10% State contribution.

These proportions describe contributions to the State funds. They should not be confused with the separate, graded cost-sharing conditions that may apply to particular assistance from national funds. For NDMF and NDRF assistance outside Response and Relief, the Commission recommended State contributions of 10% up to ₹250 crore, 20% above ₹250 crore up to ₹500 crore and 25% above ₹500 crore for other States, and a uniform 10% for North-Eastern and Hilly States.

How allocations take account of disaster risk

The Sixteenth Finance Commission's recommended method for allocating State disaster-management resources combines historical expenditure with a Disaster Risk Index (DRI). The index considers the interaction of hazard, exposure and vulnerability.

The Commission assigned 70% weight to the relevant historical expenditure measure and 30% weight to the Disaster Risk Index. Thus, allocation is not based solely on population or solely on expenditure from past disasters.

Funding-period distinction: The Sixteenth Finance Commission's 2026–31 approach should not be mixed with older allocation figures or funding-window arrangements from the Fifteenth Finance Commission period.

Prelims focus

  • Section 46: National Disaster Response Fund; Section 47: National Disaster Mitigation Fund.
  • Section 48(1)(a): SDRF; Section 48(1)(c): SDMF.
  • For 2026–27 to 2030–31, the recommended State-fund allocation is 80% SDRF and 20% SDMF.
  • The total recommended State-fund corpus is ₹2,04,401 crore for that 5-year period.
  • The general Union–State contribution ratio for Gujarat is 75:25.
  • Trap: The National Disaster Response Fund and the National Disaster Response Force are different entities.

[Sources: Government of India, Disaster Management Act, 2005, as amended through 26 December 2025, Sections 44 and 46–48; Sixteenth Finance Commission, Report for 2026–31, Volume I, chapter 11, paragraphs 11.48–11.62 and Summary of Recommendations, printed pp. 243–253; Ministry of Home Affairs, Operational Guidelines for Administration of the State Disaster Mitigation Fund and National Disaster Mitigation Fund, dated 31 July 2026, SDMF guidelines sections 1–4 and 7. Funding figures refer to the award period 2026–27 to 2030–31; status checked 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: State allocations combine 70% historical expenditure and 30% Disaster Risk Index, which considers hazard, exposure and vulnerability.
pictures.caption: The recommended State allocation method combines past expenditure with measured disaster risk.

title: India's Disaster Funds and the Sixteenth Finance Commission Framework
